newsitem.title: CANADA: Air Canada to buy Airbus A330/A340s, drop combis by 2002.
newsitem.headline: Air Canada to buy Airbus A330/A340s, drop combis by 2002.

text.p: Air Canada on Friday will announce plans to acquire up to 28 Airbus Industrie A330 and A340 wide-body aircraft, part of a plan to retire its nine Boeing 747s over the next five years, company sources told Reuters.

Air Canada has flown 747s continuously since February 1971. Only a handful of major international airlines don't fly 747s, but they include three of the biggest -- American Airlines, Delta Airlines and US Airways.
Air Canada is ordering eight A330 and A340 aircraft, and taking options on 20 more, the sources said.

The A330/340s list for $120 million ($US) each, so 28 would have a theoretical value of nearly $3.4 billion. However, Air Canada is paying substantially less, so much so that replacing six older 747s will improve the bottom line by an estimated C$20 million a year.
The Airbus contract has three phases.

Deliveries of the eight firm aircraft - five high gross weight A330-300s and three high gross weight A340-300s - will begin in October 1999, replacing three 747-100s, three 747-200s and a pair of leased, shorter-range A340s.

Subject to confirmation next March, Air Canada will become the launch customer for Airbus's stretch A340s - the jumbo A340-600 and ultra-long range A340-500, with five set for delivery starting in 2002. At that point, Air Canada gets options for 10 more.

The A340-600 can carry 360 passengers and 17 tonnes of freight up to 7,300 nautical miles, suitable for the Toronto-Osaka route. The A340-500 will carry 308 passengers on routes up to 8,300 nautical miles, such range including Toronto-Hong Kong.

Subject to confirmation in 1999, Air Canada will acquire eight more A330-300s and A340-300s for growth and to replace the airline's three Boeing 747-400 combis (combination cargo/passenger planes). Deliveries would begin as early as 2000, with the combis leaving after 2001.
Air Canada has flown 747s since 1971 and was first to fly 747-200 combis in 1972. Today, the 747s mainly fly the North Atlantic.
The 747-400s only entered service in 1991. With the extra weight of their reinforced cargo floor, they needed extra fuel to fly Vancouver-Hong Kong, limiting the amount of cargo they could carry.

The attraction of using 292-seat A330-300s to replace 414-seat 747-100s and 747-200s lies is lower operating costs. On a plane-for-plane basis, an A330-300 costs 44 percent less to fly than a 747-100, and 19 percent less on a per-seat basis. The A330 burns half as much fuel per hour.
Air Canada has been pressured by Canadian trade-union officials linked to Boeing Corp production facilities to buy Boeing's B-777 over the 330/340 to preserve jobs in the country.

Airbus won out on several counts, price, for one, but also by giving Air Canada flexibility to cancel or push back orders without penalty and to convert wide-body orders into more narrow-body aircraft.

Air Canada already operates 46 narrow-body A320s and A319s as well as eight A340s. Twenty-three more A319s are being delivered through 1998, and because of the high degree of commonality among the different Airbus lines, Air Canada can reap significant savings in maintenance, training and scheduling by adding more Airbus products and by reducing the number of fleet types.
